sources.entry: locust - Scalable user load testing tool written in Python.

summary.one_liner: Locust is an open source Python load-testing tool for HTTP and other protocols, where user test scenarios are written as ordinary Python code and run from the command line or a web UI.
summary.what_it_does: Lets you define load-test user behavior as regular Python classes and tasks, with waits between tasks and helper methods like on_start for login steps. Each simulated user runs in its own greenlet, so tests read as normal blocking Python code rather than callbacks. Tests can be run from the command line or through a web-based UI that shows throughput, response times and errors in real time, with results exportable for later analysis. The README says the load can be changed while a test is running, and that it can run headless for CI/CD. It is built on gevent, so a single process can simulate many thousands of concurrent users. Although aimed mainly at websites and services, the README says it can be extended to test other systems by writing a custom client.
use_cases: load testing a web application or REST API
writing custom load tests in Python
testing non-HTTP protocols with a custom client
real-time monitoring of response times and errors during a test
how_to_run: Write a test file defining a user class (e.g. subclass HttpUser) with @task methods
Run the test from the command line with locust, or start the web UI and open it in a browser
notable: Test scenarios are plain Python code, so IDEs and version control work as usual
Web UI shows live progress and lets you change load mid-test
Low per-user overhead, allowing very high concurrency from one process
Pluggable and hackable; the README gives examples like sending reporting data to TimescaleDB and visualizing in Grafana
Managed option on Azure Load Testing and a VS Code extension built by Microsoft
caveats: Primarily designed for web sites and services; other protocols require writing your own client
Does not solve everything out of the box; custom integrations are left to the user in Python code
Azure Load Testing and the VS Code extension are separate Microsoft offerings described in the README, not part of the core tool
